h1: Maritime NDT Consulting and Class Audit Support in Bath, Maine
html:
This page is for quality managers and NDT supervisors at fabricators, component shops and inspection firms in and around Bath, Maine, whose NDT program is about to be examined by a prime contractor, a Navy representative, a class surveyor or a customer. Atlantis NDT is an ASNT NDT Level III consulting firm: we review or rewrite the written practice, procedures and personnel files an auditor will open, run a mock audit against the checklist that auditor uses, and help you close what it turns up. To start, send us your audit notice or contract scope.

Bath's maritime economy runs through one naval shipyard

General Dynamics Bath Iron Works sits on the Kennebec River and builds Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyers for the US Navy. In May 2023 the yard laid the keel of the future USS Louis H. Wilson Jr. (DDG 126), the first Flight III destroyer it will build; Flight III ships are designed around the AN/SPY-6 air and missile defense radar. Flight IIA work has run in parallel, and the yard delivered the future USS Carl M. Levin (DDG 120) in January 2023.

For an NDT program, that concentration matters more than the size of the town. Most local inspection and fabrication businesses either work somewhere in the destroyer supply chain or compete with it for the same technicians. Structural and piping fabricators, machine shops, valve and component repairers, and inspection companies across Maine and New England take purchase orders that carry Navy technical requirements down to them. A sub-tier shop that welds a foundation, a pipe spool or a deck insert inherits the inspection rules of the ship that part goes into, and its records are judged by people who read Navy documents all day.

The rest of the Maine coast adds a second layer: smaller yards and boatbuilders that build and repair tugs, ferries, fishing vessels, research boats and yachts, and the vessels that put into Maine ports for repair. That work is governed by classification rules, Coast Guard regulations or the owner's specification rather than by NAVSEA, and it is where class approval audits for thickness measurement firms come in.

Navy work answers to NAVSEA documents, not class rules

A common mistake in shops new to defense work is treating a Navy job as a classed commercial hull with tougher paperwork. It is a different rulebook. Navy shipbuilding contracts invoke NAVSEA technical publications and military standards, and the prime passes them down in its purchase orders. For NDT the documents that come up most often are these:

  • NAVSEA Technical Publication T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, Requirements for Nondestructive Testing Methods. It sets method requirements and its own rules for qualifying and certifying NDT personnel.
  • MIL-STD-2035, the acceptance criteria that tell the technician what is rejectable on naval work.
  • MIL-STD-1689 for fabrication, welding and inspection of ship structure, and NAVSEA Technical Publication 278 for machinery, piping and pressure vessels. These decide which welds get which examinations and to what extent.

Read your purchase order before anything else. It names the documents, the revision and any contract-specific additions, and a prime's supplier-quality auditor will start from it. Our pages on NAVSEA T9074 compliance and NAVSEA NDT requirements for shipyards go further into the documents themselves. Class rules and IACS requirements do not substitute for any of this on a Navy hull, and a class approval, however useful commercially, does not qualify a firm for Navy NDT.

Two qualification schemes in one Maine shop

Many Bath-area firms take both Navy and commercial work, so they end up with technicians certified two ways: to Technical Publication 271 for Navy jobs, and to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, or CP-189 where a contract names it, for everything else. The schemes overlap but they are not interchangeable. Training content, required experience, examination structure, who may give examinations and how recertification works all differ, and an auditor from either side will check that the person who signed a report was qualified under the scheme that job required on the date the examination was done.

The tidy way to handle this is one written practice with clearly separated sections, or two companion documents, so nobody has to guess which rule applies to which job. Each certification record should name the scheme, the method, the level, the examination results, the date of the last vision check and who certified the person. Our written practice development work starts by mapping the jobs you actually perform to the scheme each one needs. The supporting files are covered on our pages about training records and certificates, experience logs and vision examination records.

Under SNT-TC-1A the company certifies its own technicians, and a course certificate is evidence of training rather than a qualification. Under the Navy scheme, who may qualify and certify is written into Technical Publication 271 itself. Either way the certifying signature belongs to your organization, and the file behind it has to show the qualification was earned.

A one-yard labor market adds its own twist. Technicians move between the shipyard, its suppliers and the inspection companies around them, and each move resets the paperwork. Under SNT-TC-1A a certification belongs to the employer that issued it, so a new hire has to be certified by your company under your written practice, using whatever prior training, experience and examination evidence that practice allows you to accept. Keep copies of what you relied on, not just a line saying the person was previously certified elsewhere.

What a prime or Navy audit of a sub-tier NDT program opens first

AreaWhat the auditor asks forGap we find most often
Contract flow-downThe purchase order, the invoked documents and revisions, and proof the shop has read themProcedures written to an older revision than the order names
PersonnelCertification records under the correct scheme, examination papers or grades, vision results, experienceExperience claimed in hours with no log or supervisor signature behind it
ProceduresMethod procedures and technique sheets for each joint type and thickness rangeA generic UT procedure stretched to cover joints it was never demonstrated on
EquipmentCalibration certificates, reference blocks, yoke lift checks, light and UV-A meter checksField checks recorded with a meter whose own calibration has lapsed
ReportsReports that tie each examination to a weld identity, procedure revision and technicianWeld numbers on the report that do not match the weld map
SubcontractorsHow the shop qualified any NDT company it hiresA subcontractor accepted on a certificate copy, with no review of its program

Our NAVSEA audit preparation checklist follows the same order, and the records retention guide covers how long to keep each kind of record.

Procedures, technique sheets and demonstrations for naval welds

Naval structure brings heavy sections, tee and corner joints, higher-strength steels and tight access that a general-purpose procedure does not handle well. A Level III earns their keep here by writing technique sheets that state the probe, angle, scan plan, sensitivity setting and reference standard for each configuration, and by running the demonstration that shows the technique finds what it is meant to find. For MT and PT, auditors look closely at the magnetizing technique and field adequacy checks, the penetrant system and dwell times, surface preparation and lighting.

Our pages on NDT procedure development and procedure qualification and demonstration describe how we structure that work. A note on radiography: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, because exposing sources requires a radioactive materials license under 10 CFR Part 34 or the equivalent Agreement State rules. As a Level III we can review your radiographic procedures and your film or digital images, while your licensed RT contractor does the exposures.

Where class approval audits fit on the Maine coast

Commercial vessels follow a separate path. A tug or ferry classed by ABS, DNV or Lloyd's Register is surveyed under that society's rules, and when its hull thickness is measured for a class survey, the gauging firm must hold that society's approval under IACS Unified Requirement Z17. The approval comes from one society, for named services, and it does not carry over to another: a firm gauging ABS and DNV ships carries two approvals and goes through two audit cycles.

The audit checks the firm's documented system, training and supervision, operator records, equipment calibration, work procedures, report formats and control of subcontracting, and it ends with a practical demonstration of the service. Thickness measurement firms are also renewed on a shorter cycle than most other service suppliers. Our IACS service supplier approval guide sets out the requirements in full; the UTM operator qualification page covers the personnel side, and our IACS UR Z17 summary walks through the requirement document.

Gauging that is not for a class survey, such as an owner checking a fishing boat's bottom plating before a sale, does not need class approval. It still benefits from the same habits: a written procedure, calibrated gauges, a trained operator and a report that another firm could repeat next year at the same locations.

Where Atlantis stands, and what it is not

We are going through the same class process we help others prepare for. Atlantis has applied to DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS for UR Z17 approval and is working through those audits now; until a society issues a certificate, Atlantis holds no class approval, and nothing on this page should be read as one. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. It is not accredited to ISO/IEC 17020 or 17025, it is not a classification society, and it is not the Navy's or your prime's auditor. Your company keeps responsibility for its quality system and for certifying its own people, and the auditor makes the decision.

Atlantis was founded by Anoop Rayavarapu, and he leads this consulting himself. His ASNT NDT Level III certificates cover five methods (VT, PT, MT, UT and RT), and behind them sit 11+ years of field work in several countries, from fabrication shops to operating plants and vessels.

How an engagement runs between Houston and Bath

  1. Scope call. We read the audit notice, the purchase order or the class application and agree what the auditor is going to cover.
  2. Remote document review. You share the written practice, procedures, technique sheets, certification files and calibration records; we mark gaps against the invoked documents and send a prioritized list.
  3. Drafting and clean-up. We draft or rewrite documents for your Level III or quality manager to approve, and set up record formats that hold up under sampling.
  4. Site visit. We travel to Bath or wherever the work is done, sample records against real jobs, watch technicians perform, and run a mock audit from the auditor's own checklist.
  5. Close-out. After the real audit we help you answer each finding with a root cause, a correction and objective evidence.

Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad. In Maine we work remotely and by site visit; there is no Atlantis office in the state. If your people also need training, see maritime NDT training for Bath and NDT training in Bath. General consulting for the area is on NDT consulting in Bath, and statewide options are on NDT consulting in Maine.

What to send us

  • The audit notice, the purchase order clauses that invoke NDT documents, or the class approval application with the society's checklist.
  • Your current written practice or practices and the list of methods and levels you certify.
  • Procedures and technique sheets, with their revision status.
  • Three or four complete job packages: weld map, NDT reports, and the certifications that were in force on each report date.
  • Calibration certificates for instruments, reference blocks, yokes and meters.
  • Earlier audit findings and how each was closed.

A readiness checklist for Bath-area NDT suppliers

  • Every certification record names the scheme (Technical Publication 271, SNT-TC-1A or CP-189) and the work it covers.
  • Vision examinations are current for every person who signed a report in the audit period.
  • Procedures match the revision of the documents invoked on the order.
  • Each technique sheet has a demonstration record or a written technical basis.
  • Weld identities on reports trace back to the weld map and forward to acceptance.
  • Subcontracted NDT is covered by an evaluation, not just a certificate copy.
  • Calibration due dates sit in one tracked list; our certificates app and the guide to equipment past calibration show one way to manage that.
  • Findings from the last audit are closed with evidence rather than promises.

For the national view of class approval audits, see maritime NDT audit support. Yard-level audit help is on Level III audit support for shipbuilding, and course options are on maritime NDT training.

faq.q: Does Atlantis audit our shop on behalf of the Navy or Bath Iron Works?
faq.a: No. Atlantis prepares you for those audits; it does not perform them. The prime's supplier-quality staff and the Navy's representatives decide whether your NDT program meets the contract. We review your documents and records, run a mock audit, and help you answer findings.

faq.q: Is a technician certified to SNT-TC-1A automatically qualified for Navy work?
faq.a: No. Navy contracts that invoke NAVSEA Technical Publication 271 apply its own qualification and certification rules. A technician can hold both, but each certification has to be earned and documented under its own scheme. We help shops lay out a written practice that keeps the two apart.

faq.q: Can Atlantis act as our outside Level III?
faq.a: Yes, as an outside agency ASNT NDT Level III in UT, MT, PT, VT and RT, for commercial work under SNT-TC-1A or CP-189. For Navy work, check what Technical Publication 271 and your purchase order require of the Level III and the examiner before you assign the role. See Level III consulting.

faq.q: Do we need UR Z17 approval to gauge a commercial tug in Maine?
faq.a: Only if the readings are for a class survey. Then the gauging firm must be approved by the society that classes that tug. Owner condition checks outside class surveys do not need it. The service supplier approval guide explains the requirement.

faq.q: Is Atlantis approved by a classification society?
faq.a: Not yet. Atlantis has applied to DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS for UR Z17 approval and is going through those audits. It holds no class approval today.

faq.q: Will Atlantis do radiography on our Navy or commercial jobs?
faq.a: No. Exposures in this country need a radioactive materials license, so Atlantis leaves radiography to licensed contractors. We can review RT procedures and images as a Level III; your licensed radiography contractor performs the exposures.

faq.q: Can the whole engagement be done remotely?
faq.a: Most of the document work can. A mock audit is stronger with a visit, because sampling records against jobs in progress and watching a technician set up shows things a file review cannot.

faq.q: What does a mock audit leave us with?
faq.a: A findings list graded by risk, with the clause or contract reference for each, the evidence we sampled, and the correction we suggest. Your quality manager decides which corrections to make. Related reading: NDT audit documentation.

faq.q: Do you write our welding procedures as well?
faq.a: That part stays with your welding engineer, who owns the WPS and the PQR behind it. Atlantis works on the NDT side and stays out of welding qualification. This WPS, PQR and WPQ explainer covers how the welding documents fit together.
Use the contact form to attach the audit notice or contract clauses plus your current written practice. Expect a reply within one business day; ours usually comes with a short list of questions.
